title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktäschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela

pages.title: Let the model look things up

blocks.html: Large pre-trained language models store a lot of facts in their parameters — but that knowledge is implicit, hard to update, and the model has no way to cite its source. When asked a factual question, the model will confidently answer regardless of whether it knows. This is the structural cause of hallucination.

RAG couples a pre-trained generator (BART) with a non-parametric retriever over an external corpus (Wikipedia). At inference time the retriever pulls top-$k$ relevant passages; the generator conditions on the query and the retrieved passages.

The key technical contribution: both the retriever and the generator are fine-tuned jointly, with the retrieved documents treated as a latent variable that's marginalized out. The retriever learns to retrieve what the generator finds useful — not just what looks superficially relevant.

Retriever: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR). Two BERT encoders — one for the query, one for the passage — produce dense embeddings; relevance is the dot product. The Wikipedia corpus is encoded offline into a FAISS index for fast nearest-neighbor search.
Generator: BART, a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence Transformer. Input is the concatenation of the query and a retrieved passage; output is the answer.
Two variants of how documents enter the output distribution:

items: RAG-Sequence: pick a single document $z$ and generate the entire answer conditioned on it. The output probability marginalizes over the top-$k$ documents: $p(y|x) = \sum_z p_\eta(z|x) p_\theta(y|x, z)$.
RAG-Token: every token in the output can attend to a different document. Marginalize over $z$ per token: $p(y|x) = \prod_i \sum_z p_\eta(z|x) p_\theta(y_i | x, z, y_{

blocks.html: RAG-Sequence is better for single-fact answers (Jeopardy, open-domain QA). RAG-Token is better when different parts of the answer need different sources.

The whole system is trained end-to-end with a standard negative log-likelihood loss on $(x, y)$ pairs. Gradient flows through the generator, and through the retriever via the marginalization weights $p_\eta(z|x)$.

The passage-encoder is held fixed during fine-tuning (re-encoding the whole Wikipedia corpus after every gradient step would be prohibitive). Only the query encoder and the generator update. The retriever learns by adjusting which documents get high probability, not what their embeddings are.

RAG sets state of the art on four open-domain QA tasks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTREC) — beating both extractive 'pick a span' models and closed-book seq2seq models (T5 with no retrieval).
On Jeopardy question generation, RAG produces more specific and factually correct questions than BART alone. On FEVER fact verification, it's within a few points of task-specific architectures.

Updating world knowledge: swap the Wikipedia index (e.g. for a more recent snapshot). The model immediately starts producing different answers for queries about facts that changed — no retraining required. This 'parametric vs non-parametric knowledge' split is RAG's main practical value.

pages.title: Why RAG became the dominant LLM application pattern

blocks.html: By 2023, 'add RAG' was the default first answer to 'how do we apply an LLM to our private documents.' The original paper's specific architecture (BART + DPR) was largely superseded by zero-shot RAG with frozen instruction-tuned LLMs (GPT-4, Claude) — but the framing it introduced — retrieval as a first-class component, treated documents as latent variables — is the conceptual foundation.

Modern descendants and variations: hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense), rerankers, hypothetical document embeddings (HyDE), graph RAG, agentic retrieval, long-context models that obviate retrieval for some use cases, and the entire ecosystem of vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma, pgvector).
